title: Starting, inviting: the hif'il
why: The second binyan of the unit: the hif'il (to start, to invite, to understand), very common in everyday life. You use it to book, order and make yourself understood at a restaurant and on the phone.

{"lessons": ["

The hif'il: doing, making something happen

One more binyan. The hif'il often expresses an action you set off or make happen: מַתְחִיל, to start; מַזְמִין, to invite, to order. In the present, it starts with מַ־ and has a long i (ִי) before the last letter: מַ + תחל → מַתְחִיל.

FormHebrewPronunciation
m. sg.מַתְחִילmatkhil
f. sg.מַתְחִילָהmatkhila
m. pl.מַתְחִילִיםmatkhilim
f. pl.מַתְחִילוֹתmatkhilot

A difference from the hitpa'el: the feminine ends in a (מַתְחִילָה), not in et (מִתְלַבֶּשֶׁת).

Compare with the previous lesson: מִתְלַבֵּשׁ, to get dressed (yourself); מַלְבִּישׁ, to dress someone (a child, for example).

A few short verbs start with מֵ־: מֵבִין (mevin, he understands), מְבִינָה (mevina, she understands).

", "

In the past and the infinitive

In the past, מַ־ becomes הִ־: הִתְחִיל (he started). With I, you and we, the i turns into a:

PronounPastPronunciation
אֲנִיהִתְחַלְתִּיhitkhalti
אַתָּההִתְחַלְתָּhitkhalta
אַתְּהִתְחַלְתְּhitkhalt
הוּאהִתְחִילhitkhil
הִיאהִתְחִילָהhitkhila
אֲנַחְנוּהִתְחַלְנוּhitkhalnu
אַתֶּםהִתְחַלְתֶּםhitkhaltem
הֵם / הֵןהִתְחִילוּhitkhilu

The infinitive starts with לְהַ־: לְהַתְחִיל (lehatkhil), לְהַזְמִין (lehazmin), לְהַרְגִּישׁ (lehargish); and for the short verbs, לְהָבִין (lehavin, to understand).

הַסֶּרֶט מַתְחִיל בְּתֵשַׁע.The movie starts at nine. [ha-seret matkhil be-tesha]
אֶתְמוֹל הִתְחַלְתִּי לִלְמֹד עִבְרִית.Yesterday, I started learning Hebrew. [etmol hitkhalti lilmod ivrit]
", "

At the restaurant, on the phone

מַזְמִין is an all-purpose verb: you invite friends, order a dish, book a table. English needs three verbs; Hebrew uses just one.

אֲנִי רוֹצָה לְהַזְמִין שֻׁלְחָן לִשְׁנַיִם.I'd like to book a table for two. [ani rotsa lehazmin shulkhan li-shnayim]
מָה אַתָּה מַמְלִיץ? — אֲנִי מַמְלִיץ עַל הַדָּג.What do you recommend? — I recommend the fish. [ma ata mamlits? — ani mamlits al ha-dag]
סְלִיחָה, אֲנִי לֹא מֵבִין. אֶפְשָׁר לְאַט?Sorry, I don't understand. Could you speak more slowly? [slikha, ani lo mevin. efshar le-at?]

With מַרְגִּישׁ, \"well/good\" stays טוֹב, even in the feminine: הִיא מַרְגִּישָׁה טוֹב (she feels good). Here, טוֹב works as an adverb: it doesn't agree.

A little word to watch for: before a definite direct object (a noun with הַ־, a first name), Hebrew adds אֶת, which isn't translated: הוּא מַזְמִין אֶת נֹעָה (he invites Noa), אֲנִי מַזְמִין אֶת הַדָּג (I'm ordering the fish). No article, no אֶת: הוּא מַזְמִין פִּיצָה. Not after a preposition either: מַמְלִיץ עַל הַדָּג.
